NAME

md_docs_2event-driven-io - Native event-driven I/O

Native server and discovery-service TCP connections use one libuv event loop per listener group. The native client adopts its connected socket into a dedicated event loop before the crypto handshake. Libuv uses epoll on Linux, kqueue on macOS/BSD, and IOCP on Windows. IOCP reports completed operations; epoll and kqueue report readiness. platform/event.h exposes asynchronous reads and writes so networking code does not depend on either model.

lib/platform/event.c owns handles, wakeups, deadlines, and worker lifetimes. lib/network/packet/decoder.c incrementally assembles ACIP headers and payloads, validates lengths before allocation, checks CRCs, and emits complete packets. lib/network/tcp/async.c implements the ACIP transport with owned output buffers and encryption. The server mode owns handshake state and media scheduling.

Ownership and shutdown

Adoption invalidates the caller's socket. Only the event loop closes it. Reads borrow a 64 KiB stream buffer; a stream worker pauses reads until its completion callback. At most one worker runs per stream. Handshakes, packet handlers, SQLite work, and client cleanup execute outside the event loop in libuv's worker pool. Render threads remain per client, but the server TCP path no longer creates per-client socket receive, dispatch, and send threads.

Writes copy caller buffers before returning and preserve enqueue order. Accepted writes invoke their completion callback exactly once, including cancellation, before the stream's close callback. Completion reports a local write, not peer acknowledgement. A successful ACIP send and the frame-send counter mean admission to the output queue. An error after encryption closes the stream because its sequence counter may already have advanced.

Shutdown stops acceptance, closes streams, cancels pending output, and drains worker and close callbacks before destroying the loop. External producers must stop before destroying their transport. The client retains a blocking receive adapter for application consumers, backed by a condition variable and complete packet queue; that consumer does not perform socket I/O.

Bounds and deadlines

  • Each stream permits at most 16 MiB or 4096 pending writes, including submitted writes. The client receive queue permits 16 MiB or 4096 packets.
  • Packet assembly, encryption workspace, and queued payloads also use the shared process buffer budget. Exhaustion rejects the operation instead of bypassing that budget with an untracked payload allocation.
  • New ASCII frames are skipped while output exceeds 256 KiB. New audio batches are skipped above 512 KiB. Already queued encrypted packets are never removed or reordered. Control traffic can use the remaining queue capacity; exhaustion terminates the connection.
  • Each loop admits at most 512 simultaneous streams and 1024 posted commands.
  • Media handshakes have a 30-second absolute deadline. Partial application packets have a 30-second deadline; receiving another fragment does not extend the current packet's deadline.
  • Discovery handshakes have a 30-second deadline, partial packets five seconds, and idle connections 60 seconds. Discovery payloads are limited to 64 KiB.

Compatibility boundaries

WebSocket and WebRTC continue to use libwebsockets and libdatachannel's event loops and their existing ACIP adapters. Browser/WASM builds do not link libuv. DNS resolution and outbound connection establishment retain the existing connection code. Outbound discovery requests retain their synchronous adapter. Native client, server, and discovery-service TCP stream I/O always uses the event backend; there is no alternate threaded TCP path or backend selection option. Linux copy avoidance is attempted automatically inside that event loop. Large writes use owned mappings and nonblocking MSG_ZEROCOPY submissions, with one outstanding submission per stream. A timer drains the error queue without blocking other connections; completion releases the mapping. Unsupported or copied submissions fall back to ordinary libuv writes on the same stream. All writes have a 30-second progress deadline; cancellation discards mappings without recycling kernel-pinned pages. This implementation does not claim a measured throughput improvement.

Build and verification

Install libuv development files (libuv1-dev on Debian/Ubuntu, libuv with Homebrew or vcpkg). The musl build fetches libuv as a static dependency.

cmake --preset default -B build
cmake --build build --target ascii-chat test-network-events
./build/bin/test-network-events
uv run --project tests/ascii_chat_tests --frozen python -m pytest tests/python/integration/event_io --ascii-chat-binary build/bin/ascii-chat
uv run --project tests/ascii_chat_tests --frozen python -m pytest tests/python/integration/network --ascii-chat-binary build/bin/ascii-chat
uv run --project tests/ascii_chat_tests --frozen python -m pytest tests/python/integration/network/test_server_client_lifecycle.py --ascii-chat-binary build/bin/ascii-chat

Use .exe executable names on Windows. The standalone test covers fragmented and coalesced packets, corrupt and oversized input, worker-driven echo, deadlines, queue saturation, and exactly-once cancellation. Integration tests exercise encrypted snapshots with stalled peers, reconnects, password, pinned identity and plaintext modes, WebSocket coexistence, automatic copy avoidance, discovery sessions, and graceful shutdown. With BUILD_TESTS=ON, the new tests register as network-events and event-io-integration in CTest.
